citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Microsoft Research AI, Carnegie Mellon University, University of Washington)
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. It consists of multiple-choice question answering pairs where, given a physical goal, a model must choose the most sensible solution from two options. The dataset contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with additional development and test sets, inspired by instructables.com and designed to test knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by majority vote, with annotators chosen who achieved 90% on the qualification HIT. Human accuracy on the development set was 94.9%.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown an instructable link as inspiration and asked to: (1) write a physical goal, (2) write a valid solution, and (3) write a "trick" — a solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT required annotators to achieve >80% accuracy on identifying well-formed vs. underspecified goal-solution pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators; users with low agreement were disqualified. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed. An interface diff button highlighted differences between solutions to improve annotator accuracy and speed.
rai:dataBiases: Reporting bias was identified as a major concern: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools (e.g., forks, knives, hammers), rarely considering the hundreds of other everyday objects. To address this, annotators were prompted with instructables links to encourage atypical solutions and flatten the distribution of referenced objects. Additionally, AFLite was applied to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples that could artificially inflate model performance.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected via crowdsourced annotation on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Annotators were provided prompts derived from instructables.com and asked to construct goal-solution pairs. Each annotator wrote a physical goal, a valid solution, and a "trick" (an invalid but plausible-sounding solution). Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions from instructables.com served as the source/seed material. Instructables is a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair, often with images or videos detailing each step and a list of required tools.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on everyday physical commonsense and excludes expert-level domain knowledge (e.g., special woodworking terminology). Some "mistakes" in model evaluation are actually correct answers that required a web search to verify. The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Future research may match human performance by finding large in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, which is not the intended use.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset was cleaned of annotation artifacts using the AFLite algorithm, which performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large, and the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances were computed. An ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets determined whether embeddings were strong indicators of the correct answer. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense, which is critical for building language models useful beyond NLP, including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The work highlights that learning about the world from language alone is limiting, motivating research into grounded, embodied AI.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking progress in physical commonsense understanding for natural language understanding models; evaluating language representations on their knowledge of physical commonsense; probing the inner workings of deep pretrained language models to determine the extent of their physical knowledge; advancing language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community (e.g., robotics).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm (using BERT-Large fine-tuned on 5,000 examples to compute embeddings for bias reduction); SpaCy (for tokenization and POS tagging of dataset statistics); GPT BPE tokenizer (for sequence length analysis)

evidence.name: we introduce Physical Interaction: Question Answering , or PIQA to evaluate language representations on their knowledge of physical commonsense.
evidence.description: In this paper, we introduce the task of physical commonsense reasoning and a corresponding benchmark dataset Physical Interaction: Question Answering or PIQA. Though humans find the dataset easy (95% accuracy), large pretrained models struggle (77%).

evidence.isLiveDataset: In total our dataset is comprised of over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional 2K and 3k held out for development and testing, respectively.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users will low agreement were de-qualed.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: Our dataset is inspired by instructables.com, which provides users with instructions on how to build, craft, bake, or manipulate objects using everyday materials. We asked annotators to provide semantic perturbations or alternative approaches which are otherwise syntactically and topically similar to ensure physical knowledge is targeted.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The instructables website is a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. In most cases, users provide images or videos detailing each step and a list of tools that will be required.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: In the HIT design the instructable provides inspiration to think out-of-the-box and annotators are asked for 1. a physical goal, 2. a valid solution, and 3. a trick. The trick should sound reasonable, but be wrong often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Additional HITs (not shown) were run for qualiﬁcation prior to this stage and validation afterwards.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Annotator pay averaged >15$/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and our timing calculations.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotator pay averaged >15$/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and our timing calculations.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of "commonsense."
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset is further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm introduced in (Sakaguchi et al. 2020; Sap et al. 2019) which is an improvement on adversarial ﬁltering (Zellers et al. 2018; Zellers et al. 2019b).
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: In practice, we use 5,000 examples from the original dataset to ﬁne-tune BERT-Large for this task and compute the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classiﬁers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether these pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: We initially experimented with asking annotators for (task, tool) pairs via unconstrained prompts, but found that reporting bias swamped the dataset. In particular, when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people most often are drawn to prototypical solutions and look for tools in the kitchen (e.g. forks and knives) or the garage (e.g. hammers and drills).
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Our goal with PIQA is to provide insight and a benchmark for progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable the construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g. special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of "commonsense."
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Philosophically, knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language. Our goal with PIQA is to provide insight and a benchmark for progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced, to enable the construction of language models useful beyond the NLP community.
